quests.correctSentence: Some people prefer big cities, whereas others love the quiet of the countryside.
quests.contrastSentence: Some people prefer big cities, therefore others love the quiet of the countryside.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whereas' joins two clauses that contrast with each other: some prefer cities, whereas others prefer the countryside. It is common in formal and written English.
quests.nativeTip: The two halves of the sentence show opposite preferences.

quests.correctSentence: The plan was risky; nevertheless, it was approved by the board.
quests.contrastSentence: The plan was risky; therefore, it was approved by the board.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Nevertheless' introduces a result that goes against expectations. 'Therefore' and 'consequently' would suggest the risk caused the approval.
quests.nativeTip: The approval is surprising given the risk.

quests.correctSentence: — Why did our prices go up? — Costs rose sharply; consequently, we had to raise them.
quests.contrastSentence: — Why did our prices go up? — Costs rose sharply; nevertheless, we had to raise them.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Consequently' introduces a result: costs rose, and as a result prices had to rise. 'Nevertheless' would signal a surprising contrast instead.
quests.nativeTip: The second half is a direct result of the first.

quests.correctSentence: Despite the heavy rain, the match went ahead as planned.
quests.contrastSentence: Although the heavy rain, the match went ahead as planned.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (the heavy rain). 'Although' would need a subject and verb: although it rained heavily.
quests.nativeTip: What kind of phrase follows the blank: a noun phrase or a full clause?

quests.correctSentence: Although she was exhausted, she finished the marathon.
quests.contrastSentence: Despite she was exhausted, she finished the marathon.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Although' introduces a full clause: although she was exhausted. 'Despite' would need a noun or gerund instead.
quests.nativeTip: A full clause follows the blank, with its own subject and verb.

quests.correctSentence: — He got the job, even though he lacked experience. — Yes, despite having no experience at all!
quests.contrastSentence: — He got the job, even though he lacked experience. — Yes, although having no experience at all!
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Despite' can be followed by a gerund: despite having no experience. 'Although' needs a subject and finite verb after it.
quests.nativeTip: The gerund 'having' follows the blank.

quests.correctSentence: The colleague with whom I share an office is very helpful.
quests.contrastSentence: The colleague whom with I share an office is very helpful.
quests.ruleExplanation: In formal English, the preposition can come before 'whom': the colleague with whom I share an office. Without the preposition, the sentence would be incomplete.
quests.nativeTip: The preposition and the relative pronoun stay together in formal English.

quests.correctSentence: The company for which he works has offices across Asia.
quests.contrastSentence: The company which for he works has offices across Asia.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'For which' places the preposition before the relative pronoun: the company for which he works. It is the formal version of 'the company he works for'.
quests.nativeTip: This is a company, not a person, and the verb 'works' needs a preposition.

quests.correctSentence: — Who is that woman? — She's the manager to whom I spoke yesterday.
quests.contrastSentence: — Who is that woman? — She's the manager who to I spoke yesterday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'To whom' is the formal way to link 'the manager' to 'I spoke to': the manager to whom I spoke yesterday.
quests.nativeTip: You speak to a person, and formal English keeps the preposition close to the pronoun.

quests.correctSentence: The company hired fifty employees, most of whom had no previous experience.
quests.contrastSentence: The company hired fifty employees, most of who had no previous experience.
quests.ruleExplanation: After quantifiers plus 'of', people take 'whom': most of whom. 'Who' cannot follow a preposition, and 'them' would create a run-on sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The relative pronoun follows 'most of' and refers to people.

quests.correctSentence: She wrote three novels, all of which became bestsellers.
quests.contrastSentence: She wrote three novels, all of whom became bestsellers.
quests.ruleExplanation: After 'all of', things take 'which': all of which. 'That' cannot follow a preposition in this structure.
quests.nativeTip: The relative pronoun refers to things, not people.

quests.correctSentence: — How were the candidates? — Twelve applied, several of whom were excellent.
quests.contrastSentence: — How were the candidates? — Twelve applied, several of who were excellent.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Several of whom' links to twelve applicants: several of whom were excellent. It is a compact way of adding extra information about part of a group.
quests.nativeTip: The candidates are people, and 'of' comes before the blank.

quests.equation: Key Form: He said he had finished the report.
quests.correctSentence: 'I have finished the report,' he said. Which is the correct reported version?
quests.contrastSentence: 'I have finished the report,' he said. Which is the correct reported version?
quests.targetWord: He said he had finished the report.
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect backshifts to past perfect: he said he had finished. 'Told' would need a person after it, such as 'told me'.
quests.nativeTip: Remember how present perfect shifts in reported speech.

quests.equation: Key Form: The museum is said to be haunted.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence means the same as: 'People say the museum is haunted.'
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence means the same as: 'People say the museum is haunted.'
quests.targetWord: The museum is said to be haunted.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Is said to be' is the standard passive form for reporting general opinion: the museum is said to be haunted.
quests.nativeTip: The museum becomes the subject of a passive structure.

quests.equation: Key Form: My bike was stolen last night.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence means the same as: 'Someone stole my bike last night.'
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence means the same as: 'Someone stole my bike last night.'
quests.targetWord: My bike was stolen last night.
quests.ruleExplanation: Passive voice fits when the agent is unknown: my bike was stolen. The bike cannot perform the action of stealing.
quests.nativeTip: The thief is unknown, so the bike becomes the subject.

quests.equation: Key Form: Should you need help, call me.
quests.correctSentence: Which is closest in meaning to: 'If you need help, call me.'
quests.contrastSentence: Which is closest in meaning to: 'If you need help, call me.'
quests.targetWord: Should you need help, call me.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Should you need' replaces 'if you need' and keeps the same meaning. It is a polite, formal opening common in business writing.
quests.nativeTip: This is the formal, inverted version of a first conditional.

quests.equation: Key Form: Had I known, I would have helped.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence means the same as: 'If I had known, I would have helped.'
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence means the same as: 'If I had known, I would have helped.'
quests.targetWord: Had I known, I would have helped.
quests.ruleExplanation: Third conditional can drop 'if' and invert 'had' and the subject: Had I known. Keeping 'if' as well would be incorrect.
quests.nativeTip: The word 'if' disappears in the inverted form.

quests.equation: Key Form: If she had studied, she wouldn't have failed.
quests.correctSentence: Which is closest in meaning to: 'She didn't study, so she failed.'
quests.contrastSentence: Which is closest in meaning to: 'She didn't study, so she failed.'
quests.targetWord: If she had studied, she wouldn't have failed.
quests.ruleExplanation: A past regret needs a third conditional: if she had studied, she wouldn't have failed. Both parts refer to the past.
quests.nativeTip: The situation is in the past and cannot be changed now.

quests.conceptTitle: Used To vs Be Used To
quests.grammarRule: Used To vs Be Used To
quests.correctSentence: When I was a child, I used to play outside until it got dark.
quests.contrastSentence: When I was a child, I am used to play outside until it got dark.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes past habits that have stopped: I used to play outside. 'Be used to' has a different meaning: being accustomed to something.
quests.nativeTip: This describes a repeated habit that no longer exists.

quests.conceptTitle: Used To vs Be Used To
quests.grammarRule: Used To vs Be Used To
quests.correctSentence: I've lived here for years, so I am used to the noise by now.
quests.contrastSentence: I've lived here for years, so I used to the noise by now.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Be used to' + noun means being accustomed to something: I am used to the noise. It describes a current state, not a past habit.
quests.nativeTip: The speaker is accustomed to the noise, and 'the noise' follows the blank.

quests.correctSentence: — Is the new schedule hard for you? — At first, but I'm getting used to waking up early.
quests.contrastSentence: — Is the new schedule hard for you? — At first, but I'm getting used to wake up early.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Get used to' is followed by a noun or gerund: getting used to waking up early. This differs from 'used to' + base verb for past habits.
quests.nativeTip: After 'get used to', the verb takes the -ing form.

quests.correctSentence: There are fewer cars on the road today than yesterday.
quests.contrastSentence: There are less cars on the road today than yesterday.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable plural nouns, while 'less' is used with uncountable nouns: fewer cars, less traffic.
quests.nativeTip: Cars can be counted one by one.

quests.conceptTitle: Common Traps: Pronoun Case After Prepositions
quests.grammarRule: Common Traps: Pronoun Case After Prepositions
quests.correctSentence: Between you and me, I think the plan will fail.
quests.contrastSentence: Between you and I, I think the plan will fail.
quests.ruleExplanation: After a preposition, an object pronoun is required: between you and me. Using 'I' here is a very common trap, even among native speakers.
quests.nativeTip: 'Between' is a preposition, so it needs an object pronoun.

quests.correctSentence: — Whom should I contact about my refund? — Contact the person who handles complaints.
quests.contrastSentence: — Whom should I contact about my refund? — Contact the person whom handles complaints.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who' is used when the pronoun is the subject of its clause: the person who handles complaints. 'Whom' is only used for objects.
quests.nativeTip: The blank is the subject of the verb 'handles'.

quests.equation: Key Form: Anna is being very patient today.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence shows that Anna's behavior is temporary and unusual?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence shows that Anna's behavior is temporary and unusual?
quests.targetWord: Anna is being very patient today.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Be' + being + adjective describes temporary behavior that differs from normal: Anna is being patient today. Simple 'is' describes her general character.
quests.nativeTip: Look for the form that describes behavior right now, not character.

quests.conceptTitle: Meaning: Present Perfect vs Simple Past
quests.grammarRule: Meaning: Present Perfect vs Simple Past
quests.equation: Key Form: I've lost my keys.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence shows that the speaker still doesn't have the keys now?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence shows that the speaker still doesn't have the keys now?
quests.ruleExplanation: Present perfect links a past action to a present result: I've lost my keys means they are still missing. Simple past can refer to a completed, unrelated event.
quests.nativeTip: Choose the tense that connects a past event to the present.

quests.equation: Key Form: He stopped to talk to her.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence means he paused in order to speak to someone?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence means he paused in order to speak to someone?
quests.targetWord: He stopped to talk to her.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Stop + infinitive' shows the reason for stopping: he stopped to talk. 'Stop + gerund' would mean he ended the conversation.
quests.nativeTip: The infinitive after 'stop' shows purpose.

quests.equation: Key Form: Had I realized how late it was, I would have called you earlier.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence is the most natural and correct?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence is the most natural and correct?
quests.targetWord: Had I realized how late it was, I would have called you earlier.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Had I realized' is an inverted past perfect, and the result clause needs 'would have' + past participle. The other options break one or both patterns.
quests.nativeTip: This uses inversion and a third conditional together.

quests.equation: Key Form: The report, which was submitted late, contained several errors.
quests.correctSentence: Which sentence is punctuated and structured correctly?
quests.contrastSentence: Which sentence is punctuated and structured correctly?
quests.targetWord: The report, which was submitted late, contained several errors.
quests.ruleExplanation: A non-defining relative clause uses commas and 'which', never 'that': the report, which was submitted late, contained errors.
quests.nativeTip: This clause adds extra information, so it needs commas and the right pronoun.

quests.correctSentence: — Why was the launch delayed? — Not only did they miss the deadline, but they also went over budget.
quests.contrastSentence: — Why was the launch delayed? — Not only they missed the deadline, but they also went over budget.
quests.ruleExplanation: After 'not only' at the start, the auxiliary comes first: not only did they miss the deadline. This closes Stage 9 by combining inversion with everyday workplace language.
quests.nativeTip: This opening phrase changes the word order that follows.
